Programmed obsolescence
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_obsolescence
You could design a car that runs for 300K miles. In fact the old Toyotas were probably over engineered in this regard.
The problem is if you can restrict the useful life to about 100K at which point break downs and repairs make the car a hassle, you can get people to buy 3-4 cars in the same span. Modern cars are designed to degrade over time for this very purpose.
As an aside no car will run forever. Due to constant cycling which induces warming and cooling which leads to fatigue as well as the friction involved in the process every car will eventually break down but what we see now is cars designed not for maximum length of service but for conforming to consumer expectations (5-6 years and 100k miles) which ensures that as soon as you pay off your last car loan it's time to buy a new car. Add onto this a known lemon ratio (every mass manufacture has one due to broader design tolerances) and you have a strong disincentive to not buy used cars in favor of cheaper less durable new cars.

[edit]
New cars are basically designed to require the minimal maintenance during the 100k window with no expected replacement parts other than one change of breaks and tires. Their interiors rely on cheap plastic that will slowly dry out and crack over time.

Age is worse than high mileage in most cases. Modern engines don't really wear out like they used to for the most part. Some have innate flaws that can manifest at any mileage. Ford and their timing chains for example or Subaru and their head gaskets.

100k miles as being old is kinda throwback to the past. Personally I think 200k is the new 100k for most non-throwaway cars.

I would also add, much depends on how well the previous owner had the car maintained. Cars are machines that require regular maintenance. If the maintenance hasn't been done on schedule you could be looking at a car with just 50K miles on it that may not be worth the risk. A well maintained higher mileage car might be a better investment. However, I personally feel a low mileage three year old car that has been maintained is always a better investment than a new car.
